newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Rebel Dnestr region defies Moldova in poll.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Dnestr region defies Moldova in poll.

text.p: Moldova's Dnestr separatists voted on Sunday in a presidential election aimed at showing its independence from the rest of the country, which chose its new president on December 1.
Dnestr's two presidential hopefuls are current leader Igor Smirnov, 55, elected Dnestr president in 1991, and Vladimir Malakhov, 44, a lesser-known local company manager.

Tall and balding, Smirnov is seeking re-election for another five years. He is a Soviet-era industrial manager who used to run one of the region's biggest factories and is viewed as sure winner of the poll.
"Our state exists de facto... These elections are another step towards the legal recognition of our state," Smirnov told reporters after voting in central Tiraspol, the Dnestr capital.
Malakhov had offered voters very similiar separatist rhetoric. "My political programme does not differ much from Smirnov's," he said after voting.
Most Dnestr residents, who streamed to polling stations where sandwiches were provided and pop music boomed out of loudspeakers, said they would vote for Smirnov.
"Smirnov set up our republic and defended it. If it were not for him, we would have already been turned into Romanians," said pensioner Ivan Moroz, 67.

Dnestr, a depressed industrialised strip of land in Moldova's east along the Ukranian border, broke away in 1990 on fears its mostly Slav residents could be sidelined in Moldova's eventual merger with ethnic kin in neighbouring Romania.
Hundreds were killed in a bloody war between Moldovan security forces and Dnestr separatists in 1992. The bloodshed was stopped by the intervention of Russian troops.
Suffering from economic hardships stemming from the lack of reforms -- rapid elesewhere in Moldova -- local residents are nostalgic for "stable Soviet times" and seek support from Russia.

"I want to be closer to Russia... I dream of cheap bread and clothes, and I want my pension to be raised," said Moroz. His pension, paid in Dnestr's worthless coupon currency, is only enough to buy 50 portions of bread rationed in Dnestr.
Russia is involved in the rebel region through the presence of its 6,000-strong troops, and Smirnov promises to let them stay "as a guarantor of security", if re-elected.

Moldova's talks with Dnestr over its future status, mediated by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Russia and Ukraine, are stalemated over separatist demands for full independence. Moldova offers broad autonomy.
"We do not want to be given something by Moldova... If Moldova wants to live with us in friendship and harmony, it should treat us as a state," Smirnov told reporters.
But Moldova remains adamant on the issue of its integrity.
"These elections will have no political or legal effect," Moldova's president-elect Petru Lucinschi has said.
